title: Sushi, Dim Sum and Wood-Fired Pizza Reach Delhi-NCR's Street Carts
excerpt: A new generation of thela owners in Noida, Delhi and Gurgaon is selling restaurant dishes at street prices — four pieces of sushi for Rs 220, Neapolitan pizza from Rs 280, and mutton gosht with parottas on weekends.
body:
• Street carts across Delhi-NCR now sell sushi, dim sum, wood-fired Neapolitan pizza and mango sticky rice alongside golgappe and chaat, an India Today survey of vendors found.
  • Prices undercut restaurants sharply: a four-piece vegetarian sushi plate starts at about Rs 220 against dine-in prices from Rs 500, and cart pizzas run Rs 280 for eight inches to Rs 600 for ten.
  • Named carts include Steam Bites and Sushi Senpai in Noida's Sector 76 (the latter rolls until 3 am), International Food Haven in Gurgaon, Gusto Italiano's wood-fired pizzas, and Laham by Shabfoods' weekend mutton gosht.
  • Founders invested between Rs 30,000 and Rs 4 lakh to start; all told India Today their carts are now profitable, though vending-zone space and 40-50 minute peak waits remain problems.

The street-food order in Delhi-NCR is changing. Next to the golgappe and aloo tikki chaat, carts now roll sushi, steam har gow-style dim sum and blister wood-fired Neapolitan pizzas with puffy, charred crusts — dishes that until recently meant booking a restaurant table. India Today reports that even Delhi's Ramlila melas had sushi stalls this year, and some carts serve well past midnight.

Sushi and dim sum in Sector 76

The cluster is densest in Noida's Sector 76 market. Prachi Bhalla founded her dim sum cart, Steam Bites, after a meal at the Japanese restaurant Kylin made her wonder why dishes she could learn to make at home cost Rs 1,000 to Rs 1,500 in a restaurant.

"We wanted to sell them at a fraction of restaurant prices and make them more accessible."

— Prachi Bhalla, founder, Steam Bites

In the same market, Prabal Tiwari and Rohan Kumar opened Sushi Senpai after a meal at YouMee convinced them sushi could be sold for less; their cart keeps rolling until 3 am. In Gurgaon, Gaurav Bhareja and his wife run International Food Haven, serving Korean, Thai and Japanese dishes including mango sticky rice. Bhareja told India Today the cart format itself is the draw: customers watch ingredients being added and the food being made live, and get more interested in eating it. A four-piece vegetarian sushi plate starts at about Rs 220 and an eight-piece non-vegetarian portion goes up to Rs 550, against dine-in prices starting around Rs 500.

Pizza from a wood fire, gosht from Rajasthan

At Gusto Italiano, friends Kartavya and Puneet, both in their mid-20s, serve Neapolitan pizzas, calzones and garlic bread until 12:30 am. Puneet learned the craft from an Italian couple, Max and Jennifer; the sauce is made two to four hours ahead with tomatoes imported from Italy, seasoned only with oregano, salt and basil, and the dough travels to the cart in an icebox. Prices run from about Rs 280 for an eight-inch pizza to Rs 600 for a ten-inch. The meat course belongs to Laham by Shabfoods, a weekend-only cart run by two former product managers, Rishab and Shashi Kant, selling Namkeen Gosht sourced from Rajasthan with bite-sized Malabar parottas at Rs 149 for a half plate and Rs 250 for a full one. Rishab says their mutton volume has grown tenfold in a month, from 2.5 kg to 25 kg.

The hard part is not the cooking

Every vendor prepares sauces, dough and fillings hours ahead in separate small kitchens and refrigerates ingredients, because a cart has no room to do it on site. Customers are the second challenge: Bhalla says people regularly look at her dim sum and ask for momo, so the difference — a rice or potato starch wrapper, different fillings, four variants — has to be explained plate by plate, and Bhareja offers first-timers a half plate before they commit. Bhareja also tried Thai curry on the cart and dropped it for lack of demand. Location is the third problem: some Noida vendors say they have been moved on after noise and traffic complaints and operate outside designated vending zones while allotments lag — a claim India Today said it had not independently verified. And a 25-order queue at Laham can mean a 40-50 minute wait standing on a pavement, with none of a restaurant's air-conditioning to soften it.

The economics, for now, work. Bhalla invested about Rs 1-1.5 lakh in Steam Bites, Gusto Italiano's founders roughly Rs 3-4 lakh, and Laham's founders Rs 30,000-50,000 — and all of them told India Today the carts are profitable, powered largely by young customers arriving with a saved Reel and a new appetite. The golgappe, the vendors promise, are not going anywhere. They just have neighbours now.
